html:
SMTO-GIT-0003 — SMTO couldn't read this Git project's setup

GUID: 21955c30-036c-4453-a53f-3d46362c6de0
Slug: git-repository-incomplete
Domain: GIT · Subsystem: git

What happened

  • After a Git command, SMTO tried to note which project folder was used, but that folder's hidden Git information is incomplete or damaged. Your command's result wasn't changed; SMTO just won't remember this project.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask SMTO in this conversation to run git status in the same project folder, and read what Git reports. If Git also reports an error, the folder's Git information really is damaged, not just SMTO's check of it.
  2. If Git reports an error, get a fresh copy of the project (for example, clone it again into a new folder) instead of editing the hidden .git files by hand. A fresh copy has complete Git information, so both Git and SMTO can recognize the project.
  3. If Git works normally but this message keeps appearing, open Technical details in this panel and select Copy error details. The exact message shows whether the hidden .git file or a missing Git file stopped SMTO's check.

What success looks like

  • git status runs in that folder without errors, and this message no longer appears after your next Git command there.

If it still fails

  • Send the copied error details and the folder's path to the person who manages the computer running the Gateway. Don't delete the hidden .git folder or file; it holds the project's history.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Gateway Git discovery rejected the repository: the .git file lacks the 'gitdir: ' prefix, the resolved Git directory has no HEAD file, or the common directory has no config file.

What this means

  • A .git file lacks the gitdir prefix, or resolved metadata lacks the required HEAD or common config file. These checks validate repository identity/observation. Failure of an optional observation does not establish failure or rollback of the Git command whose receipt carries it; no diagnostic rewrites Git metadata.

Why this can happen

  • A .git file lacks the gitdir prefix, or resolved metadata lacks the required HEAD or common config file.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the gitfile target, common directory and required files with ordinary Git tooling without overwriting them.

How to fix it

  • On the Gateway host, inspect the .git entry at the repository root, the HEAD and commondir files in the resolved Git directory, and config in the common directory, using git rev-parse --git-dir --git-common-dir and git status. Restore missing metadata from a trusted clone or recreate the worktree (git worktree repair or a fresh clone); SMTO never rewrites Git metadata and this observation failure does not alter the Git command's own outcome.
  • Inspect the repository and its gitfile/worktree target with ordinary Git tooling. Restore the intended repository metadata from a trusted source before refreshing discovery.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended repository's metadata is intact and ordinary Git and discovery agree.

What not to do

  • Do not remove retained state or weaken trust checks to make an unavailable dependency appear healthy.

Technical notes

  • These checks validate repository identity/observation. Failure of an optional observation does not establish failure or rollback of the Git command whose receipt carries it; no diagnostic rewrites Git metadata.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
